name: Dave
summary: Dave is a banking app built around two things: a Dave Checking account and a small cash advance called Extra Cash, worth up to $500. Almost everything in the app is organized around one decision made early on, connecting the bank account a user is already paid into, since that connection is what Dave uses to decide advance eligibility, and it's also one of the things the $1 monthly membership pays for. Saving happens through round-ups on Dave's own debit card, which flow into a Goals account created automatically the first time round-ups are turned on. Getting paid faster by moving direct deposit to Dave does double duty: it's marketed as arriving up to 2 days early, and it's also how an advance eventually gets repaid.
teaser: A cash advance and checking app where saving, borrowing, and getting referred all wait on the same bank connection to clear.

observations.name: Pre-account screen leads with an amount and two removals
observations.observed: The first screen presents the brand mark and then loads a headline offering up to $500 when the user needs it, qualified by "No interest, no credit check". The same screen shows a rendering of the product's card and two buttons, Login and Sign up for Dave.
detail: The headline amount is $500.
The two qualifiers are stated as no interest and no credit check.
An asterisk on the headline links to a "See terms" control.
No third option, guest mode, or demonstration path is shown on this screen.

observations.name: The headline's terms sit behind an asterisk
observations.observed: Tapping "See terms" opens a pop-up restating the $500 headline and then describing the product underneath it: Extra Cash is a demand deposit account with overdraft utility, an advance results in a negative balance, the advance is subject to eligibility, and delivery fees may apply. The pop-up refers the user to the account agreement for details and closes with a "Got it" acknowledgement.
detail: The negative-balance consequence of an advance is disclosed here and not in the headline.
Eligibility is named as a condition here and not in the headline.
Delivery fees are named as possible here and not in the headline.
The pop-up is dismissed by acknowledgement rather than by acceptance.

observations.name: One sign-up path, with consent bundled into the continue action
observations.observed: Sign-up opens with "First create a sign in ID", requiring an email address and a password, and no alternative registration method is offered at this point in the session. Below the fields, text states agreement to the privacy policy, terms of use and electronic communication consent, and the user proceeds with a single "Agree and continue" button.
detail: Email and password are the only credentials collected at this step.
Consent to three separate documents is carried by one button.
No separate checkbox is shown for these three consents.
The absence of a social or third-party sign-in option is stated by the analyst as applying at least at this moment.

observations.name: Legal name is requested as a distinct step
observations.observed: The next screen reads "Let's get started. What's your legal name?" and collects first name and last name.
detail: The word "legal" is used at this stage, before identity documents are mentioned.
First and last name are separate fields.

observations.name: Phone number is requested with a security justification
observations.observed: The following screen reads "Nice to meet you. What's your mobile phone number?" and explains that the number is used to protect the account with two-factor verification.
detail: The stated purpose of the number is account protection.
A "Next" action advances from the field.

observations.name: A marketing consent is placed on the verification-code screen
observations.observed: The verification screen states that a six-digit code has been sent to the provided number and offers a resend control and a code entry area. Below the code field, the screen carries an agreement to receive special offers and promotions by SMS at the same number, with the standard qualifiers that consent is not a condition of purchase, rates may apply, frequency varies, and STOP unsubscribes.
detail: The marketing consent appears on the same screen as the security step it is separate from.
The number used for verification is the number the marketing consent applies to.
The consent text links to terms of use and privacy policy.
Whether the consent is a checkbox, a toggle, or carried by the continue action is not established in the session.

observations.name: Biometric login is offered with an explicit skip
observations.observed: The next screen asks whether the user wants to use Face ID to log in, offering "Yes, sign in with Face ID" or "Skip for now". Choosing the biometric option raises the operating system permission prompt.
detail: A skip is offered on the same screen as the acceptance.
The skip is worded as deferral rather than refusal.

observations.name: An app passcode is created regardless of the biometric choice
observations.observed: The user is then asked to create a four-digit app passcode and to re-enter it on the following screen.
detail: The passcode is four digits.
Confirmation is a separate screen rather than a second field.
Whether the passcode step can be skipped is not shown.

observations.name: The bank connection request is justified by the size of the approval
observations.observed: The next screen reads "Connect your primary bank" and asks the user to connect the account they are paid into so the product can determine their best approval amount. The same screen states that advances can be received instantly for a small fee.
detail: The requested account is specified as the one the user is paid into.
The stated benefit of connecting is a better approval amount.
Instant delivery is introduced as a paid option at the moment of connection.

observations.name: The membership charge is authorised on the bank connection screen
observations.observed: Below the connection request, the same screen carries an agreement to the recurring payment authorisation for the $1 monthly membership fee.
detail: The recurring charge is $1 per month.
The authorisation shares a screen and a continue action with the bank connection.

observations.name: The bank connection step has three exits
observations.observed: The screen offers "Agree and continue", a separate "I don't have a bank account" path, and a dismissal control in the top right corner. The analyst records that the step is therefore not required.
detail: Two of the three exits leave the account unconnected.
What the product does after either non-connecting exit is not shown.

observations.name: A second screen restates the fee alongside what it buys
observations.observed: After continuing, a screen headed "Connect your bank and debit card" states that the $1 monthly membership fee keeps the bank account connected, sends low balance alerts and provides budgeting tools. Below this, the screen numbers the remaining work as connecting the bank account and linking that account's debit card.
detail: Three named benefits are attached to the fee: connection, low balance alerts, budgeting tools.
The fee is restated on a second consecutive screen.
The remaining work is presented as two numbered steps.

observations.name: Bank connection is handed to a third party with trust framing
observations.observed: The connection is performed by Plaid, introduced on a screen stating that 8,000 apps trust Plaid, that connection takes seconds, and that best-in-class encryption protects the data. Within that flow the user enters a phone number or continues as a guest, verifies the number by code, selects the account to share, and logs in to their bank.
detail: The count stated is 8,000 apps.
A guest path avoids giving the phone number to the connection provider.
Before the bank login, the screen lists the boxes to check at the bank: the checking or prepaid account, bank account numbers, and account holder information.
The data listed is what the bank will be asked to share onward.

observations.name: The linking wait carries product claims
observations.observed: While the account links, a progress screen presents claims rather than status detail: that paying members lowered their overdraft fees by nearly 70%, and that the product helps over 11 million members stay on top of their finances. The screen also states that transactions are being analysed.
detail: The overdraft claim is attached specifically to paying members.
The membership figure stated is over 11 million.
These claims appear at a point where the user cannot act.

observations.name: The debit card is linked with its settlement purpose stated
observations.observed: The next step asks the user to add and link the debit card associated with the connected bank account, stating that this card may be used to settle any advances taken. The completed state shows the linked bank and the linked card together.
detail: The card must be associated with the connected bank account.
The stated function of the card is settlement of advances.

observations.name: The first dashboard is empty except for one prominent action
observations.observed: After connection, the home screen greets the user with "start building your financial future" and presents an "Open checking account" button, with further options below. The bottom navigation carries four destinations, Home, Account, Extra cash and Grow, and a settings control sits in the top right corner.
detail: The primary call to action on first entry is opening a second account rather than using the connected one.
The navigation has four tabs.
The analyst records difficulty reading what sits under the primary button on this screen.

observations.name: The checking account is pitched twice before any identity request
observations.observed: Tapping "Open checking account" opens a screen headed "Get more with Dave" describing a checking account with no minimum and no overdraft fees, no monthly fees and no balance requirements, phrased as "Ditch fees for good". A "Get started" action advances to a second pitch screen.
detail: The pitch leads with removals rather than additions.
Three fee-related claims appear on this screen: no minimum, no overdraft fees, no monthly fees or balance requirements.
No identity information is requested before this point in the flow.

observations.name: The second pitch screen introduces saving, funding and access
observations.observed: The next screen, headed "Save with Dave in every way", describes rounding up spare change on purchases toward financial goals, transferring money between external accounts at any time, and depositing cash at over 90,000 locations with fee-free deposits at two named retailers. Listed below as other benefits are instant advances, fee-free withdrawal at over 37,000 ATMs, sending cash and checks, digital and physical debit cards, 24/7 real-time support, and FDIC insurance through the partner bank.
detail: Round-ups are introduced here, before the account exists.
The deposit network is stated as over 90,000 locations, with fee-free deposits named at Walgreens and CVS.
The ATM network is stated as over 37,000.
The partner bank is named as Evolve Bank and Trust, member FDIC.
The FDIC coverage figure is not legible in the session record.

observations.name: Date of birth is the first identity field
observations.observed: After "Get started", the first identity screen reads "Confirm your identity. When were you born?" and collects a date.

observations.name: The tax identifier is requested with a legal reason and a security reassurance
observations.observed: The next screen requests the Social Security number, states that US federal law requires this information to verify identity, and collects the number twice. Beneath the fields, the screen states that the entry is protected by bank-level security.
detail: The requirement is attributed to federal law rather than to the product.
The number is entered twice.
A security reassurance sits directly under the most sensitive field in the flow.

observations.name: A review screen precedes submission
observations.observed: A "Review your info" screen restates legal name, date of birth, Social Security number and residential address, prefaced by a warning that the information must match the user's identity documents. The user confirms from this screen.
detail: Residential address appears on the review screen although its collection is not shown in the session.
The warning is marked as important.

observations.name: Identity confirmation runs as a timed wait
observations.observed: After confirmation the product displays "Confirming your identity. This may take a couple minutes. Hang tight.".
detail: The wait is described in minutes rather than seconds.
No alternative action is offered during the wait.

observations.name: Account opening carries a credit reassurance and a single checkbox
observations.observed: The next screen, "Let's open your account", states that this will not affect the user's credit. It presents a Dave Checking account option described as spending instantly with no hidden fees, and a checkbox by which the user agrees to the checking deposit agreement, its disclosures and the partner bank's privacy policy, before the "Open Dave Checking Account" action.
detail: The credit reassurance is placed immediately after the tax identifier and identity check.
One checkbox carries agreement to three documents.
A "See terms and conditions" link is present.

observations.name: The opening wait is filled with value propositions
observations.observed: While the account opens, the screen displays "Opening your account" and cycles value propositions as content loads, including spending instantly with the digital card and making purchases and paying bills with the digital debit card. The sequence ends with confirmation that the checking account is set up.
detail: The propositions appear during an unavoidable wait.
The propositions concern the card rather than the account terms.

observations.name: Funding is requested immediately after the account exists
observations.observed: The next screen, "Add money to your Dave checking account", offers setting up direct deposit with the claim of being paid up to two days early, transferring from another bank in four to five business days, and depositing cash fee-free at two named retailers with a barcode. A "Not now" option is available.
detail: Three funding routes are presented together with their speeds.
Direct deposit is the only route carrying a speed advantage claim.
The deferral option is present on the same screen.

observations.name: The account home is a balance widget with immediate actions
observations.observed: The Dave Checking screen shows a widget with the available balance, a control to view the debit card, and Add money and Withdraw actions, with an "Add to Apple Wallet" button below.
detail: Balance, card access and money movement occupy the same widget.
Wallet provisioning is offered at the top level rather than inside card settings.

observations.name: The physical card delay is bridged by a digital card
observations.observed: A notification states that the physical debit card should arrive by a stated date and instructs the user to use the digital card while waiting, with a "View digital card" control.
detail: The arrival date is presented as a specific date.
The exact date is not legible in the session record.
The waiting period is given a usable substitute rather than only an explanation.

observations.name: Digital card controls include a freeze that is off by default
observations.observed: The digital card screen displays the card and offers a toggle to show card information and a toggle to freeze the card, which is off by default, with controls below to set the PIN and replace the digital card, and an "Add to Apple Wallet" action at the bottom. Wallet provisioning offers a choice of phone or watch and requires accepting terms and confirming.
detail: Freeze is present as a user-operated control.
Freeze defaults to off.
Replacing the digital card is available without a support contact.

observations.name: The empty activity state instructs rather than describes
observations.observed: Recent activity reads "No activity yet" followed by "Get started by using your Dave Checking account" and a statement that all activity will appear there.
detail: The empty state names the action that would fill it.

observations.name: A hub groups six banking utilities under one entry point
observations.observed: Scrolling the checking screen reveals "Do more with Dave Checking" listing direct deposit, recurring transfer, scan or send a check, deposit cash, withdraw cash and pay bills. Below it sit two further prompts, setting up direct deposit to be paid up to two days early, and starting a budget with the product's budgeting tool.
detail: Six utilities are grouped in one hub.
Direct deposit appears both inside the hub and as a separate prompt below it.
The budgeting tool is surfaced here as a prompt; its own screens are not entered in the session.

observations.name: Round-ups are introduced as a setup flow with reversibility stated up front
observations.observed: A section headed "Save every time you spend with Roundup" states that purchases are rounded up to the nearest dollar every time the product's debit card is used, that round-ups automatically roll into a Goals account, that the user can contribute additional money at their own pace, and that they can take their savings out or pause at any time. Links to learn more and to the goals deposit agreement sit below, before a "Get started" action.
detail: The trigger is any purchase on the product's own debit card.
The rounding rule is to the nearest dollar.
The destination is a separate Goals account rather than the checking balance.
Withdrawal and pausing are stated on the introduction screen, before opt-in.
The analyst records uncertainty about how this section is reached from the preceding screen.

tags.name: Piggy Bank
tags.rationale: The product accumulates identifiable units of value in a reserve held separately from the account the user spends from, and it does so through repeated automatic contributions triggered by ordinary activity. Round-up amounts are taken from purchases made on the product's own debit card and roll into a Goals account that the product creates as a precondition of the automation (tier: directly observed). Goals is listed as its own account alongside checking and extra cash, carries its own available balance, and the product describes the release of that value as taking savings out (tier: directly observed). That the value is restricted from ordinary spending while it sits in Goals is not stated in a single sentence anywhere in the session; it follows from the account separation, the separate balance, and the described withdrawal action (tier: strongly supported). The library's own boundary case for an automatic round-up savings pot resolves in favour of this entry on the same structure, and the reserve holding real user funds rather than bonus rewards does not remove the invariant. The surface passes the engagement-design test independently of being stored value: the product creates the goal for the user, sets a default target, shows a progress bar, prompts a first deposit with minimising language, and offers recurring deposits framed as reaching goals faster (tier: directly observed).
tags.alternativeConsidered: That the Goals account is an ordinary savings sub-account and therefore commerce infrastructure carrying no mechanic label. The separating evidence would be whether the Goals balance can be spent directly, for example by card or bill payment, without a transfer back to checking. If it can, the reserve is not restricted and the entry does not apply. The session does not test this, which is why the restriction sits at strongly supported rather than directly observed.

observations.name: Round-ups cannot exist without a Goals account
observations.observed: Continuing opens "Open your goals account to start using Roundup", stating that a goal will be created for the user's debit card purchases to round up into. The user selects a Dave Goals account, described as personal savings for financial milestones, and agrees to the goals deposit agreement and disclosures before creating the account.
detail: The savings container is created as a precondition of the automation, not the reverse.
A goal is created by the product rather than by the user at this step.
One checkbox carries the deposit agreement and its disclosures.

observations.name: Adding money prices the funding source and confirms by swipe
observations.observed: From the widget, "Add money" collects an amount and then presents a source choice: a bank account with no fee, or Apple Pay with a 1% fee. The transfer screen carries a recurring toggle, and the transfer is committed by swiping a control from left to right, after which the product confirms and states arrival in four to five business days.
detail: The fee difference between sources is stated at the point of choice.
The confirming action is a swipe rather than a tap.
The arrival window for the transfer is four to five business days.
The completion screen carries a prompt asking whether the user wants to be paid up to two days early by setting up direct deposit.

observations.name: The recurring transfer toggle is on by default within the recurring flow
observations.observed: Choosing "Recurring transfer" from the hub collects an amount and a source, and the recurring toggle is already on rather than requiring the user to enable it. The user then selects a frequency, weekly or other, and a day, and agrees by checkbox to a recurring transfer of the stated amount on the stated day, referencing the recurring payment authorisation agreement. The transfer is committed by swipe and the product reports it as set up.
detail: The toggle state is on by default when the flow is entered from the recurring-transfer entry point.
Frequency options observed are weekly and a further unspecified option.
The full set of frequency options is not established.
Cancellation is performed by turning the same toggle off, and the analyst records that this cancels it.

observations.name: Direct deposit offers three routes, one of them tagged as fastest
observations.observed: The direct deposit screen is headed "Earlier paydays are easy with Dave" and repeats the up-to-two-days-early claim, then presents three routes: finding the employer, which carries a "fastest" tag and signs the user into their company's pay portal; copying and pasting the account details into the employer's portal manually; and sending HR a form that the product generates from a few questions. A footnote states that early access depends on the timing and availability of payroll files from the payer and that funds can be available up to two business days in advance of the scheduled payment date.
detail: Three routes are offered for the same outcome.
Only one route carries a speed tag.
The employer-search route is handled by a third party, Pinwheel, introduced with encryption, credential-privacy and speed claims.
The copy-and-paste route surfaces the account details for manual entry elsewhere.
The early-access claim is qualified by a dependency the product does not control.

observations.name: The form route asks how much of the paycheck to move
observations.observed: The send-HR-a-form route collects the employer name and then asks how much of each paycheck the user would like to deposit, stating that this can always be changed later, with two options: deposit full paycheck or deposit part of paycheck.
detail: A partial option is presented alongside the full option rather than only as a later adjustment.
Reversibility is stated in the same sentence as the question.
The mechanism for specifying the partial amount is not shown.

observations.name: The generated form is pre-signed by default option and can be routed two ways
observations.observed: The next screen states that the form is filled out and can be sent by the user or straight to the employer, with a checkbox offering to pre-sign the form, and two buttons, send to my employer or send it to myself. After sending, the product confirms that the direct deposit form has been emailed to the user's address and offers to resend or finish.
detail: Pre-signing is offered as a checkbox rather than a separate signing step.
Whether the pre-sign checkbox is checked by default is not established.
Both routes end with an email confirmation to the user.

observations.name: The accounts tab separates the product's accounts from the connected one
observations.observed: The Accounts tab lists the product's own accounts, Dave Checking, Goals and Extra Cash, and lists the external checking account separately below them.
detail: Three internal accounts exist by this point in the session.
The external account is presented in its own group.
Opening the external account shows its available balance, the linked debit card, a prompt to start a budget, and recent transactions.

observations.name: Check handling is split into scan and send, each with its own speed and fee
observations.observed: The scan-or-send-a-check entry opens a chooser: scanning a check takes ten days with no fee or is instant for a fee, and sending a check arrives within five business days with no fee. The scanning route hands over to a partner, Ingo Money, described as processing the checks the product cashes, with options to cash a check or learn more. The sending route asks who the check should go to and maintains recipients.
detail: Scanning offers a free slow path and a paid instant path.
Sending has one speed and no fee.
The check-cashing partner is named in a dedicated introduction screen.
Recipients can be added within the send flow.

observations.name: Cash deposit is free at two named retailers and priced elsewhere
observations.observed: The deposit-cash flow begins with location selection, stating that fee-free deposits are at CVS and Walgreens using a barcode scan and that other locations may charge a service fee. The next steps describe following on-screen prompts and scanning an in-app barcode or swiping the card, keeping the receipt, and expecting the deposit to post typically within ten minutes and up to thirty at some locations. A "See locations" control opens a map of the nearest cash deposit places.
detail: Two retailers are named as fee-free.
A service fee ceiling is stated for other locations.
The stated fee amount is not legible in the session record.
Posting time is stated as typically ten minutes and up to thirty at some locations.

observations.name: Cash withdrawal is presented as a map with per-location instructions
observations.observed: The withdraw-cash entry opens a map listing nearby ATM and cash withdrawal locations. Selecting one shows the full address and opening hours with two actions, get directions and how to withdraw cash. The instruction screen describes inserting the card, entering the four-digit card PIN, and following the ATM prompts.
detail: Location data and procedural instruction are placed on the same surface.
The PIN referred to is the debit card PIN of four digits.

observations.name: Bill payment offers three routes without leaving the account
observations.observed: The pay-bills screen offers paying with the debit card by copying its details for online payment, paying from the checking account by copying the routing number, account number and partner bank details, or sending a check from the checking account for no fee arriving within five business days.
detail: Three payment routes are offered for the same outcome.
Each identifier can be copied individually.
The check route restates the no-fee and five-business-day terms.

observations.name: The product creates the user's first goal and gives it a target
observations.observed: After the goals account is created, the screen reads "Your goals account is ready for roundups", states that round-ups are set up for the new goal, and invites the user to personalise it by editing title, goal amount and end date. Opening the goal shows the goal detail, with the savings target set by default at $75 and round-up switched on.
detail: The goal exists before the user has defined anything about it.
The default target amount is $75.
Round-up is already on for this goal.
Three attributes are named as editable: title, goal amount, end date.
A "Set a recurring deposit" control sits below, framed as reaching goals faster.

observations.name: Personalisation is offered before any money is in the goal
observations.observed: The goal detail screen allows editing the title and the goal amount, changing the appearance of the banner image, and viewing the savings figure.
detail: The banner image is editable from the goal detail screen.
Personalisation is invited at a point when the goal balance is zero.

observations.name: The goals surface shows a balance, a yield and a progress bar
observations.observed: The Goals entry in the accounts list opens a screen showing the available balance for goals, a 4% APY figure, and a progress bar for savings. A "Get started, add some money" prompt and an "Add money" control appear, with "Create a new goal" below.
detail: The yield stated is 4% APY.
A progress bar represents position against the goal amount.
Whether reaching the goal amount produces any recognition, message or state change is not shown.

observations.name: Additional goals share a single ceiling with existing ones
observations.observed: Creating a new goal asks for a name and then a goal amount, stating that the amount can be set up to $24,925. The session records that the ceiling is the $25,000 limit less the $75 already held in another goal.
detail: The stated overall limit is $25,000.
The offered maximum for the new goal is reduced by the existing goal's amount.
The limit is expressed only through the reduced maximum, not as a separate statement of remaining capacity.

observations.name: Goal appearance is chosen from an external image library
observations.observed: The goal creation flow offers "Add a photo to represent your goal", and selecting it opens Unsplash, from which the user chooses an image before creating the goal.
detail: The image source is a third-party image library rather than a built-in set.
The stated purpose of the image is to represent the goal.
The image is attached to the goal, not to the account or the user profile.
The image does not alter any stated goal rule, limit or rate in the session.

observations.name: The first deposit prompt uses small presets and minimising language
observations.observed: After the goal is created, the screen reads "Start achieving your goal" and states that tiny amounts will quickly add up, so the user should not be afraid to kick things off with just a few bucks. It offers three preset first deposits of $5, $25 and $50, a custom amount, and "Maybe later" at the bottom.
detail: The lowest preset is $5.
The copy addresses reluctance rather than benefit.
The deferral option is present and is placed last.
Choosing "Maybe later" still completes goal creation.

observations.name: Ending a goal is permanent and cascades into the automation

observations.name: Ending a goal is immediately followed by an offer to restart the automation

tags.name: Earning Tasks
tags.rationale: The product presents, inside its own Grow tab, a catalogue of discrete compensated tasks supplied by a named third party, inBrain AI, and directs payment into the product's own checking account (tier: directly observed). Each listed survey carries both a payout and an estimated completion time before the user begins it, which is the entry's per-task disclosure of compensation and effort; the payout figures for the longer recommended surveys are not legible in the session record, but the quick surveys are listed at $0.45 for about 8 minutes and $0.50 for about 10 minutes and the listing form is the same for every item (tier: directly observed). The entry requires at least one continuation element layered over the individual tasks, and three are present: a monthly earnings total displayed above the list, an ordered division of the catalogue into recommended, other and quick-survey sections, and the stated progression that higher paying surveys unlock as the user continues (tier: directly observed). The entry's own borderline case describes this exact configuration and resolves in favour of the label. The commercial arrangement itself is excluded by the entry and carries no label here: the supplier relationship, the terms toggle, and the deposit into the checking account are commerce infrastructure and are described in Pass One in plain language (tier: directly observed).

The separating evidence is whether a continuation element exists independently of the payment relationship. tags.name: Referral Boost
tags.rationale: The product identifies the user as someone who can introduce another person and provides the route, offering controls to share or copy a referral link (tier: directly observed). It defines an action the referring user performs and can perform again, the extra cash advance, and it requires a completion event from both parties: the referring user must have taken and repaid an advance, and the introduced person must repay one, with the product stating explicitly that the qualifying event is the friend's repayment rather than their sign-up (tier: directly observed). Satisfying both conditions grants an enhancement expressed relative to the referring user's own future advance, 20% more up to $100 more, which is a larger amount of the same action rather than a payment (tier: directly observed). Nothing in the session presents the boost as a balance, credit or item the user could hold, spend or transfer; the product describes it only as more on an advance (tier: directly observed). That the enhancement is realisable only by taking another advance, and not separable from it, follows from that framing rather than from any observed application (tier: strongly supported). The entry's own borderline case covers a boost described in copy but never seen operating and resolves presence in favour of the label under the operating card's presence standard, which is why the tag is applied at strongly supported rather than withheld; how the boost is actually delivered is recorded as unresolved below.
tags.alternativeConsidered: That the boost is a held credit the user could apply elsewhere, in which case the entry's second exclusion sends it to the applicable currency or credit entry instead. The separating evidence is a session in which a boost is earned and the referring user then takes an advance: if the enhancement appears as a credited balance or as a payment separable from the advance, this tag should be withdrawn. Gifting was also considered and set aside, since the sender directs no benefit to the recipient and neither party's balance changes by an act of the sender.

proposedTags.name: Scheduled eligibility re-check
proposedTags.draftDefinition: When a user requests a gated benefit and does not qualify, the product declines without closing the request, names a recurring interval at which the decision will be reconsidered, and offers a notification for the moment eligibility changes.
proposedTags.conditions: A benefit gated by a system-evaluated eligibility rule; a decision the product will re-evaluate rather than treat as final; a named interval short enough to be actionable; a notification opt-in offered in place of the withheld benefit; a stated or implied route by which the user can change the input the decision depends on.
proposedTags.whyNotCovered: No approved entry describes a refusal that carries a return date. Daily Login Rewards requires a benefit granted for access rather than a re-evaluated decision. Daily / Weekly Quests requires an objective instance with a completion state, and no objective is issued here. The behaviour is a return trigger built on a pending decision rather than on a reward or a task.
proposedTags.recurrenceElsewhere: Lending, credit-limit increases, insurance underwriting, marketplace seller eligibility, waitlists and account-upgrade flows all decline provisionally and invite a return. The structure is describable without reference to this product.
proposedTags.caveat: The session observes the refusal, the named interval and the notification offer, but not a single re-evaluation. Whether the decision is genuinely reconsidered daily, and whether the interval is a real cadence or a phrase, is not established.

proposedTags.name: Assisted external redirection
proposedTags.draftDefinition: The product provides several parallel routes for completing a required action inside a third-party system it does not control, including at least one route in which the product generates the paperwork on the user's behalf, and offers a partial-commitment option so the user need not move the whole of the thing being redirected.
proposedTags.conditions: An action outside the product's control that materially changes the product's value to the user; more than one route to that action, differentiated by effort or speed; a route in which the product does the work and the user only supplies identifying details; an option to commit part rather than all; a statement that the choice can be changed later.
proposedTags.whyNotCovered: No approved entry addresses the product assisting an action performed in another system. The behaviour is not a quest, a challenge or an achievement, because the product neither issues an objective nor records a completion state; it reduces the cost of a step it cannot perform.
proposedTags.recurrenceElsewhere: Payroll redirection, utility and insurance switching, subscription migration, number porting and pension transfer flows all take this shape. The structure is describable without reference to this product.
proposedTags.caveat: The session shows the routes and the partial option but no completed redirection, and it does not show how the partial amount is specified. Whether the pre-signature checkbox is on by default is also not established, and that default bears on any definition of the assisted route.

systemView: The product is organised so that one connection decision made during onboarding governs almost everything that follows.

Connecting the account the user is paid into (O9, O13) is the input to the eligibility determination for the advance (O56), which is the product's headline offer on its first unauthenticated screen (O1) and again on its own tab (O51). That same connection is one of the three things the $1 monthly membership is said to pay for (O12), and the membership also pays for the low balance alert (O82), which is the product's most frequent reason to reopen the app (O81). The membership charge is authorised on the connection screen itself (O10), so the fee, the connection and the eligibility path are agreed in one action.

The advance sits behind a gate the session never passed (O54). Everything downstream of it therefore also sits behind that gate. The referral reward is not cash but a larger next advance (O71), and its first qualifying step is that the referrer has taken an advance (O73), so the growth loop cannot start until the eligibility loop resolves. The settlement mechanism for an advance is the next paycheck (O52) and the linked debit card (O15), which gives the direct deposit flow (O35, O36, O37) a second function beyond the two-days-early claim it advertises: it makes the paycheck arrive where settlement happens.

The savings side runs on a different dependency. Round-ups are triggered only by purchases on the product's own debit card (O31), which requires the checking account (O17 to O23), which requires the identity verification sequence (O19, O20, O21). Round-ups in turn require a Goals account (O32), so the savings container exists as a precondition of the automation rather than as something the user asked for, and the first goal arrives already created with a $75 target and round-up switched on (O43). Ending a goal cascades back into that automation, pausing round-ups and cancelling recurring transfers (O49), and the product answers the cascade immediately with an offer to restart it by creating another goal (O50). The savings surface and the spending surface are therefore coupled in both directions: spending feeds saving, and removing the savings target switches the feeding off.

The Grow tab connects the two halves. Survey earnings are paid into the checking account (O59), which is also the settlement point for advances and the source of round-ups, so a user who earns in Grow is funding the same account that both the saving automation and the borrowing settlement depend on. The job board within Grow points outward (O69), but its featured position is occupied by the product's own survey surface (O68), which points back in.

Dependencies worth stating plainly. O54 depends on O9, O13 and O56. O71, O72 and O73 depend on O54. O31 depends on O17 through O23 and on O28. O43, O45, O46, O47 and O48 depend on O32. O49 and O50 depend on O31 and O34. O82 depends on O12 and O13. O59 and O61 depend on O23. O35, O36 and O37 depend on O23 and feed O52.

What the session cannot say. It observed no advance, no repayment, no referral boost, no goal reaching its target, no survey completing and no notification arriving. Six of the nine dependency chains above terminate in behaviour that was never seen, and every one of them terminates at the same place: the eligibility decision the product deferred to tomorrow.

sectionLeadIns.onboarding: This section covers everything between opening Dave for the first time and reaching the empty home screen. It runs through the pitch before signup, identity verification, and connecting a bank account and debit card.
sectionLeadIns.growth: This section covers Dave's referral program: where it sits in the app, what it pays, and the steps involved in earning it.

sectionCards.onboarding: Dave walks new users through signup, identity checks, and connecting a bank and debit card before showing an empty home screen.
sectionCards.core-loop: Dave runs everything through the checking account once it exists: adding money, moving money, direct deposit, round-ups, checks, cash, and bill pay.
sectionCards.goals: Dave creates, personalizes, extends, and ends a user's savings goals.
sectionCards.access: Dave pitches, explains, and gates the Extra Cash advance behind eligibility.
sectionCards.earning: Dave pays users for surveys and a profiling questionnaire, and points them to outside jobs through a board of its own.
sectionCards.social: Dave has no feature that lets a user see, interact with, compare against, or team up with another identified person.
sectionCards.growth: Dave runs its referral program from settings and pays it out as a bigger future advance.
sectionCards.money: Dave charges for membership, advance delivery, funding, cash and check handling, and pays interest on two of its accounts.
sectionCards.returns: Dave brings users back through notifications, balance alerts, and a marketing consent gathered during signup.
